idiom_name: @main/App-init or didFinishLaunching bootstrap (+ stored properties are eager, static let is not)
implementation_notes: Swift gives you half of the mechanic for free and hides the other half: stored properties are initialised when the instance is created, which is the eager form, while a static let is initialised lazily on first access with once semantics, so 'declared at file scope' does not mean 'acquired at launch'. Eager acquisition therefore means doing the work in a phase you control - @main's initializer, the app delegate's didFinishLaunching, or a bootstrap function called from either - and forcing any static let you rely on. Concurrency follows the same rule as promises: an unstructured Task begins executing when it is created, so the launch path must await the warm-up task before reporting readiness, and URLSession configuration (waitsForConnectivity, pre-warmed connections) is the platform-level version of the same decision.
pitfalls: lazy var is not thread-safe - there is no lock - so a warm-up touched from two threads can build the value twice or publish a partially initialised object; use a stored property or an explicitly forced static let.
A static let written exactly where eagerness is wanted is still initialised on first access, so code that assumes launch-time acquisition silently keeps the cold path.

Doing the acquisition synchronously in App.init or didFinishLaunching spends the launch budget: exceeding the watchdog limit kills the app, and long work there blocks the main thread before the first frame.
